title: Rule of Three, Five and Zero
objectives: Name the six special member functions and state which ones the compiler generates, deletes or omits given the ones you declare
Explain why a user-declared destructor silently removes implicit move operations
Implement a correct Rule-of-Five resource-owning class (deep copy, safe assignment, noexcept move, self-assignment safe)
Apply the Rule of Zero: compose classes from RAII members so no special members are declared at all
motivation: A class that owns a raw buffer looks innocent until the compiler copies it: the implicit copy constructor copies the *pointer*, two objects now delete the same memory, and you are back in the previous lesson's double-free debugging session. The rules of three, five and zero are the design discipline that prevents this: which of the six special member functions must you write, when does the compiler's implicit set become dangerous, and why is declaring nothing (rule of zero) the goal for most classes?

blocks.md: C++ gives every class up to six special members: the **default constructor**, **destructor**, **copy constructor**, **copy assignment**, **move constructor** and **move assignment**. You write none of them, the compiler may generate them implicitly; you write one, and the compiler's decisions about the others change - sometimes silently. The historically dangerous case: declare a destructor (say, to free a buffer or just to log), and the compiler still generates **implicit copy operations** that copy member-by-member - for a raw pointer that is a shallow copy, two owners, one delete. Worse, the implicit **move operations are simply not generated**, so every apparent move is a hidden copy. Your code compiles and behaves 'reasonably' until the aliasing bites.

blocks.text: Rule of Three - and the bug it prevents

blocks.md: **Rule of Three** (pre-C++11): if a class needs a custom destructor, a custom copy constructor or a custom copy assignment, it almost certainly needs **all three** - the presence of one signals that the class manages a resource the defaults mishandle. Watch the default copy alias the buffer:

blocks.caption: The implicit copy constructor copies the pointer; the destructor pair then frees it twice.

blocks.text: Rule of Five - the full contract

blocks.md: Since C++11, the three grow to **five**: destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment. A resource-owning class defines all five (or deletes some) so that every operation is deliberate. Two details separate correct implementations from subtly broken ones. First, assignment operators must handle **self-assignment** (`a = a`) and must free the old resource only *after* the new data is secured - the version below allocates the replacement first, giving the strong guarantee. Second, move operations must be **noexcept**: vector promises not to use a throwing move during reallocation (it would break the strong guarantee), so a non-noexcept move silently degrades reallocation to copies.

blocks.caption: The five members, each deliberate: deep copy, safe assignment, noexcept steals that leave the source empty.

blocks.md: The moved-from Buffer is deliberately **valid but empty**: `data_ == nullptr`, `n_ == 0`. Assigning to it or destroying it is fine - that is the contract move operations must uphold, because vector reallocation moves elements and later destroys the husks.

The best resource-owning class is one that does not own raw resources at all: compose it from members that already manage themselves - `std::vector`, `std::string`, `std::unique_ptr`. Declare **none** of the six special members, and the compiler-generated operations are correct by construction: copies deep-copy because members deep-copy, moves move because members move, destruction releases because members release. This is the **Rule of Zero**, and it is the goal: rule of five is for library authors writing containers, rule of zero is for everyone else.

blocks.caption: No special members, no bugs: the members carry the whole resource-management burden.

blocks.title: The logging destructor that killed performance
blocks.md: A team added `~Order() { log("order destroyed"); }` to trace lifetimes - and reallocation of `std::vector<Order>` slowed 40x. Declaring the destructor suppressed the implicit move operations, so every reallocation copied every Order (strings, vectors and all) instead of moving. Fix: `~Order() { log(...); }` stays, but the class gains `Order(Order&&) = default; Order& operator=(Order&&) = default;` - and the copy operations are then implicitly deleted, which is exactly what you want for an RAII type.

Two keywords complete the toolkit. `= default` asks the compiler to generate a member it would otherwise have suppressed - the standard way to keep moves alive after declaring a destructor. `= delete` forbids a member entirely: delete the copy constructor of a connection class and attempts to copy it fail at compile time with a clear message, turning the double-close bug into a build failure. Explicitly defaulting the destructor (`~T() = default;`) also documents intent without changing behaviour.

blocks.caption: The whole lesson in one picture: implicit copy aliases the heap block (double free); a correct move leaves the source empty and the single owner unambiguous.

hints: `T x = expr;` initialises a NEW object - that is a constructor, never assignment.
Assignment applies to an object that already exists (b was built before).
Destruction of locals happens in reverse construction order: c, then b, then a.
guidedExercise.solution:
Output: `ctor copy move copy= move= ~ ~ ~ `

- `Probe a;` → **ctor**.
- `Probe b = a;` initialises b from a: **copy** constructor (assignment never constructs).
- `Probe c = std::move(a);` initialises c from an rvalue: **move** constructor.
- `b = a;` assigns to the existing b: **copy=**.
- `b = std::move(c);` assigns an rvalue: **move=**.
- At scope exit, destruction runs in reverse construction order: **~** for c, **~** for b, **~** for a.

Note that assigning from the moved-from `a` in `b = a;` is legal - a is valid, merely unspecified as to content.

independentExercise.prompt: class Ticket owns a C resource: `FILE* f_` opened in the constructor, closed in the destructor. (a) List exactly what goes wrong with the compiler-generated copy and move operations. (b) Write the Rule-of-Five version using `= default` and `= delete` wherever the compiler's version is already correct. (c) Then rewrite the class to reach Rule of Zero, holding the resource as a member `std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, decltype(&fclose)> f_` - and state what remains to be written by hand.
hints: (a) Both copies would close the same FILE* twice; what would the implicit moves even do here?
(b) The destructor body is the only hand-written member; everything else is a policy statement.
(c) unique_ptr with a function-pointer deleter calls fclose at destruction - what is left is construction policy, not cleanup.

commonMistakes: Declaring a destructor (even just for logging) and unknowingly losing implicit move operations - copies silently take over in vector reallocation.
Writing operator= that assigns members before releasing the old resource - self-assignment or a throwing copy then corrupts or leaks.
Handling self-assignment only in the copy assignment and forgetting it in the move assignment.
Omitting noexcept on move operations: std::vector falls back to copies during reallocation, quietly erasing the optimisation.
Applying Rule of Five to classes composed of self-managing members - declare nothing instead (Rule of Zero) and let the members work.
realWorldApplication: Code review for resource-owning classes is a checklist against these rules: does it own anything raw? then all five members are visible and deliberate. Does it compose from containers and smart pointers? then none of the six are declared. Almost every C++ style guide encodes exactly this decision procedure.
quantFinanceApplication: A position class holding a raw fill-history buffer without Rule of Five double-frees the first time a desk copies it into an archive; the Rule-of-Zero rewrite (vector + unique_ptr members) ships with zero resource-management code - and the move operations it gets implicitly are what make rebalancing pipelines cheap.
summary: Six special members: default ctor, dtor, copy ctor/assign, move ctor/assign; what the compiler generates depends on what you declare.
Declaring a destructor keeps implicit copies (deprecated) but suppresses implicit moves - 'moves' become hidden copies.
Rule of Three (dtor + copy ctor + copy assign) governs pre-C++11 resource classes; Rule of Five adds noexcept move ctor and move assign.
Correct assignment secures new resources before releasing old ones, handles self-assignment, and move operations leave the source valid but empty.
Rule of Zero: compose from RAII members and declare nothing - correct copies, moves and destruction come for free.

quiz.explanation: a's ctor prints 'd'; `A b = a;` is initialisation, so the copy ctor prints 'c'; `b = a;` is assignment to an existing object: 'ca'. At scope exit locals die in reverse order: b then a, printing '~~'. Total: d c ca ~ ~.

quiz.prompt: A class gains a user-declared destructor. What happens to its implicit copy and move operations (C++17)?
options: Copies and moves both remain implicit
Copies remain implicit (deprecated), move operations are not generated - apparent moves become copies
Copies are deleted, moves remain implicit
Both copies and moves are deleted
quiz.explanation: Declaring any of the five suppresses implicit moves; implicit copies are still generated for a destructor-only declaration (deprecated behaviour). This is why a 'harmless' logging destructor can quietly replace moves with copies in containers.

quiz.prompt: Which members make up the Rule of Five?
quiz.explanation: Rule of Five = destructor + copy ctor + copy assign + move ctor + move assign. The default constructor is not part of the rule (it is one of the six special members, but resource management turns on the other five).

quiz.prompt: When does the Rule of Zero apply?
options: Whenever the class allocates memory with new
When all resources are held by self-managing members (vector, string, unique_ptr) so no special members are declared
When the class deletes all copy and move operations
Only for classes with no data members
quiz.explanation: Rule of Zero = declare none of the six special members and compose from RAII members; the generated operations are then correct because the members' operations are correct.

`B b = a;` copy-constructs (C); `B c = std::move(a);` move-constructs (M); `b = a;` copy-assigns (A); `b = std::move(c);` move-assigns (X). Initialisation uses constructors; assignment to existing objects uses operator=.

quiz.prompt: Why must a move constructor be marked noexcept for a class stored in std::vector, and what happens if it is not?
quiz.modelAnswer: vector guarantees the strong exception guarantee during reallocation; it only moves elements if the move is noexcept (via move_if_noexcept), otherwise it copies them so a throwing move can roll back. A non-noexcept move therefore silently degrades reallocation to copies - correctness is kept, but the optimisation is lost.
quiz.explanation: vector::resize/push_back growth moves elements only when the move cannot throw; otherwise copying preserves the strong guarantee. The cost of forgetting noexcept is performance, not correctness.

flashcards.front: What are the Rule of Three and Rule of Five?
flashcards.back: Three: destructor, copy ctor, copy assign - if you need one, you need all three. Five: plus move ctor and move assign (C++11), with moves marked noexcept.

flashcards.front: What does declaring a destructor do to implicit copy/move operations?
flashcards.back: Implicit moves are NOT generated (so moves degrade to copies); implicit copies are still generated (deprecated). Use = default to restore moves.
Compose classes from self-managing RAII members (vector, string, unique_ptr) and declare none of the six special members - generated operations are then correct by construction.

flashcards.front: A Buffer class has `int* data_; ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }` and uses the implicit copy ctor. Bug?
flashcards.back: Shallow copy: two Buffers own one pointer, both destructors delete it - double free. Fix: Rule of Five (deep copy + moves) or Rule of Zero (std::vector<int> member).

flashcards.front: Why is noexcept required on move operations used inside containers?
flashcards.back: vector reallocation moves elements only if the move cannot throw (strong guarantee); a throwing move falls back to element-by-element copying.
